caption: capacity factor of coal held open by federal order, Jan–Aug 2026
headline: Coal held open by federal order ran at 22% of capacity this year; coal its owners kept ran at 38%.
text: KPA matched every delayed unit to DOE's orders and its owner's filings, then measured its output in EIA's generator data through August. The units held by orders ran at 22% of capacity in January–August 2026, down from 49% in the same months of 2022–24. Units their owners kept ran at 38%, up from 34%, against 47% for the US coal fleet.
source: KPA's comparison of ordered units, owner-kept units and the fleet, from EIA-923 and EIA Form 860M data (fleet figure from EIA's Electric Power Monthly). Falling output at the ordered plants was reported earlier by Utility Dive (23 June 2026), Argus (30 March 2026) and MV2 (19 October 2026), and is credited.

caption: of coal listed a year ahead retired in the year listed, 2016–24
headline: For a decade, EIA's coal retirement dates were a dependable forecast: 88% of the capacity listed a year ahead retired on time.
text: KPA traced every coal unit in EIA's December inventories for 2015 to 2023 to its status in September 2026. Of the 57.4 GW listed to retire the following year, 88% retired in the year listed, and 97% has retired since; even in the weakest year, 2023, 73% went on time. In 2025, 27% did.
source: KPA's own calculation, pooled across 2016–24, from EIA Form 860M inventories. MV2 (Munim, Inc.) reported earlier, in October 2026, that 26% of the 2025 list retired on time against 72% or more in earlier years, and is credited; KPA's 27% uses September 2026 net summer capacity.

caption: of the 8.1 GW of delayed coal is held by federal emergency orders
headline: Federal orders hold less than half of the coal whose retirement has slipped; owners and grid contracts hold the rest.
text: Of the 8.1 GW of coal whose 2025 or 2026 retirement date has passed or moved past 2026, DOE's orders cover 3.7 GW, or 46%. Owners, or their contracts with grid operators, kept the other 4.4 GW. The largest is Brandon Shores in Maryland, 1.3 GW that Talen Energy runs under a reliability-must-run contract with PJM until May 2029.
source: KPA's own split, pooled across 2025 and 2026, from EIA Form 860M, DOE's orders and owners' filings. EIA (13 April 2026) split 2025's delays and MV2 (October 2026) split 2026's; both are credited. Taken one year at a time, orders hold the larger share of 2025's delays.

caption: per megawatt-day: Campbell's net cost under federal order
headline: Net of market revenue, keeping the Campbell plant open has cost about $460 per megawatt-day, 1.4 times PJM's capped capacity price.
text: Consumers Energy reports that Campbell has cost $303 million through September, net of $344 million in market revenue, or about $611,000 a day. Spread over the plant's 1,331 MW, that is about $460 per MW-day: 1.4 times the $325 cap at which PJM's latest capacity auction cleared, and about twice MISO's annualized capacity price for 2025–26.
source: KPA's own calculation from Consumers Energy's Form 10-Q (27 October 2026); the cost and revenue totals are Consumers' own. On DOE's larger 1,560 MW rating, the figure is $392.

caption: more coal in 2029 than the schedule assumes, at 2025's follow-through
headline: If owners treat the 2027–28 schedule as they treated 2025's, the United States will enter 2029 with about 14 GW more coal than its own schedule assumes.
text: Setting aside the TVA units its board voted to keep, 16.3 GW of the 2027–28 schedule remains. If it follows 2016–24, about 14.4 GW retires; if it follows 2025, about 4.4 GW; if it follows 2026 to date, almost none. About 14 GW is about as much as the United States retired in 2022, its largest year since 2015.
source: KPA's own scenarios, applying its follow-through rates from EIA Form 860M to the September 2026 schedule. Not found in KPA's prior-publication search.

caption: of coal scheduled to retire in 2027–28, none of it under an order
headline: The coal scheduled to retire in 2027–28 ran at 42% of capacity this year, harder than the coal owners have already kept.
text: EIA lists 18.3 GW to retire in 2027–28, 11% of the 167.8 GW US coal fleet, and none of it is under a federal order. The group ran at 42% of capacity in January–August 2026, and 8.3 GW of it ran at or above the fleet average, among them Rockport unit 1, Monroe, Baldwin and Cardinal unit 3. TVA's board has already voted to keep 1.9 GW of it.
source: KPA's own analysis of EIA Form 860M (September 2026) and EIA-923 generator data. TVA's decision is from its board vote of 11 February 2026, reported by Utility Dive and Industrial Info Resources.

caption: of US coal retired in 2025, against 9.8 GW a year in 2015–24
headline: US coal retirements fell to 2.7 GW in 2025, the least since 2010, and to none in the first nine months of 2026.
text: In 2015–24, the United States retired an average of 9.8 GW of coal a year. In 2025 it retired 2.7 GW, the least since 2010, though only just below 2011. EIA's September inventory records no coal retirement of any kind in 2026. Owners have moved 2.8 GW of the 2026 list past the end of the year.
source: KPA's own count from EIA Form 860M (September 2026). EIA (23 February 2026) counted 2.6 GW retired in 2025 on a different basis, and MV2 (Munim, Inc.) reported earlier, on 16 and 29 October 2026, that no 2026 coal had retired; both are credited.

caption: January capacity factor of the units then under order, Stanton aside
headline: In January, when the grid was tightest, most of the plants held as insurance did not run hard.
text: The units under orders in January, Stanton aside, ran at 32% of capacity that month, and Centralia and Craig produced nothing; Craig was under repair until 20 January. The owner-kept units ran at 44%. Campbell was the exception: it ran at 59% for the month, slightly above the fleet's 58%, and DOE says it ran above 650 MW every day during Winter Storm Fern.
source: KPA's own calculation from EIA-923 generator data for January 2026; Campbell's Winter Storm Fern output is DOE's own figure (6 February 2026). Argus (30 March 2026) reported January output at Centralia and Craig earlier and is credited.

caption: per megawatt-hour: Schahfer's net cost under order, first quarter 2026
headline: Under federal order, the Schahfer plant cost about $118 for each megawatt-hour it produced in the first quarter of 2026.
text: NIPSCO has asked to recover $38.0 million, net, for the first quarter of 2026, when one derated unit ran for two months: about $118 for each megawatt-hour it produced. Schahfer unit 18 has been out since a rotor blade failed in July 2025.
source: KPA's own arithmetic from NIPSCO's cost-recovery filing to FERC (4 August 2026) and EIA-923 generator data; the $38.0 million is NIPSCO's own figure.

caption: of coal at the fleet's rate would match the ordered units' output
headline: The orders keep 3.7 GW of coal available, but its output this year could have come from 1.7 GW.
text: At the US fleet's rate of use, the ordered units' 2026 output could have come from 1.7 GW of coal. The orders ask for availability, not output: each directs the owner to keep the unit ready and to run it when the grid operator finds it cheaper than the alternatives. In EIA's inventory, every one of these units is listed as operating.
source: KPA's own calculation from EIA-923 generator data and EIA's Electric Power Monthly. MV2 noted earlier that the orders require availability, not generation, and is credited.

caption: of gas EIA lists as not seeking approval is approved or building
headline: EIA's status codes lag the field: 41% of the gas it lists as not yet seeking approval is already approved or under construction.
text: KPA checked each of the 35 plants behind the 37.4 GW that EIA lists for 2027–30 as not yet seeking approval, against regulators' orders, utility filings and company statements. Of that capacity, 15.4 GW, or 41%, is already approved or under construction. Another 5.8 GW is before regulators.
source: KPA's own analysis: a plant-by-plant check of EIA Form 860M (September 2026) against state commission dockets, utility and company releases, SEC filings and trade press.

caption: GE gas equipment on order or reserved, 30 September 2026
headline: GE Vernova's gas book has more than doubled in 18 months.
text: Of GE's 122 GW, 64 GW was firm orders and 58 GW was reservations at the end of September, up from 50 GW in total at the end of March 2025. GE expects at least 130 GW by the end of the year.
source: Reported figure, not a KPA finding: GE Vernova third-quarter 2026 release, 28 October 2026.

caption: about mid-year: when GE's planned output equals its current book
headline: At GE's planned output, the current book equals production through about mid-2031.
text: At 20 GW a year, 122 GW is about six years of production; GE plans 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030. On 28 October, GE said it had sold several slots for delivery in 2032.
source: KPA's arithmetic on GE's stated output plan, a measure of size rather than a delivery date. XenoSpectrum (20 October 2026) first reported the years-of-output ratio and is credited.

caption: growth in planned US gas capacity, September 2024 to September 2026
headline: Planned US gas capacity rose 3.5 times in two years while the share under construction fell.
text: Planned gas rose from 20.6 GW in September 2024 to 71.1 GW in September 2026 in EIA's inventory. Capacity under construction rose only from 5.4 GW to 13.1 GW, so its share fell from 26% to 18%.
source: KPA's own analysis of EIA Form 860M; the under-construction share is KPA's own. EDF and Atlas Public Policy (13 October 2026) and Frontier (23 September 2026) reported similar rises and are credited.

caption: extra cost of planned combined-cycle plants at 2025 costs
headline: At 2025 costs, the planned combined-cycle fleet would cost at least $31 billion more than at 2023 costs.
text: KPA applied BloombergNEF's cost rise (from under $1,500 to $2,157 per kW) to the 47 GW of combined-cycle capacity in EIA's planned list. That is slightly more than major US utilities spent on transmission in all of 2023, though the premium would be paid over several years of construction.
source: KPA's own calculation from BloombergNEF and EIA data. A lower bound, because BloombergNEF puts 2023 costs under $1,500/kW.

caption: of gas listed two years ahead was canceled or postponed
headline: Gas listed a year ahead has almost always been built; gas listed two years ahead often has not.
text: KPA traced every gas generator on four earlier EIA lists to its status in September 2026, counting only plants whose planned year has passed. Of capacity listed about a year ahead, 94–100% is operating; of capacity listed about two years ahead, 35–46% is operating and 39–62% was canceled or indefinitely postponed.
source: KPA's own analysis of four EIA Form 860M inventories. Related completion rates by Cleanview (2025), LBNL (Queued Up, 2026) and munimv2 (October 2026) are credited.

caption: GW signed per GW shipped, Q2 to Q3 2026
headline: GE's signings fell toward its shipments in the third quarter.
text: In the second quarter, GE signed 6.7 GW of new gas contracts for each gigawatt it shipped; in the third, 2.2, partly because shipments rose from 3 GW to 5 GW. A falling ratio can mean buyers are running out of near-term slots to reserve, or the rush to reserve is cooling.
source: KPA's own calculation from GE Vernova quarterly releases. The fall in reservations, from 63 GW to 58 GW, is GE's own disclosure.

caption: GW of 2028–30 merchant gas plans at risk on the past record
headline: On the past record, 10–16 GW of merchant gas plans for 2028–30 would drop off EIA's list.
text: Applied to the 25 GW of 2028–30 plans held by independent producers, the record would put 10–16 GW at risk, and 10.4 GW of those plans are Project Matador. The record is small, four groups and 22 GW, so it is a yardstick rather than a forecast.
source: KPA's own calculation from its lead-time base rates for EIA Form 860M.

caption: of the turbine contract often put down, non-refundable per GE
headline: Buyers carry risk from the first deposit, not from conversion to a firm order.
text: Customers have often put down 20–25% of the turbine contract, and GE's chief financial officer said in October 2025 that the deposits are non-refundable for reservations and firm orders alike. Data centers account for about 20% of GE's gas book but about a third of its reservations.
source: Reported figure, not a KPA finding: GE Vernova earnings calls (23 April 2025, 22 October 2025, 28 October 2026), Bank of America conference (18 March 2026) and 2025 Form 10-K.

caption: Project Matador alone: about 18% of US gas planned for 2027–30
headline: One data center campus, Project Matador in Texas, is about 18% of all US gas planned for 2027–30.
text: Of the 37.4 GW EIA lists as not yet seeking approval, 19.5 GW, or 52%, would serve a named data center campus. Only Matador's first phases, about 1 GW, are under construction; the other 10.2 GW has no signed buyer.
source: KPA's own analysis from its plant-by-plant check of EIA Form 860M. Global Energy Monitor has tracked gas proposals tied to data centers and is credited.

caption: of net US demand growth, 2014–23, came from data centers
headline: Data centers were roughly all net US demand growth, 2014–23.
text: Between 2014 and 2023, US data centers increased their electricity use by about 118 TWh. Over the same nine years, total US retail sales rose by only about 110 TWh. Everything else combined was essentially flat, within 1%. Ending the comparison in 2025, data centers account for about 60% of growth.
source: KPA calculation on Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and EIA data. Range across estimates: 73–108%. The general point, that data centers drive growth, was published by EIA and IEA.

caption: the growth of 2021–27 against the 14 years before
headline: Growth in 2021–27 is ten times the prior 14 years.
text: Retail electricity sales were 3,765 TWh in 2007 and 3,806 TWh in 2021. EIA expects 4,217 TWh by 2027, a gain of about 411 TWh in six years against 41 TWh in the fourteen before.
source: Arithmetic on EIA Monthly Energy Review and October 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook. Similar multiples were published earlier (Creaspace, September 2026).

caption: when a large gas turbine ordered today would run, per EPRI
headline: The plant arrives after the forecast window closes.
text: EPRI finds the largest gas turbines now take more than five years from order to delivery, so one ordered today would, on average, not run until 2031. KPA's point is the timing: that is after the 2025–30 window over which utilities forecast the demand it is meant to serve. GE Vernova disputes the bottleneck, putting new heavy-duty orders at about three years.
source: The 2031 date is EPRI's (B. Noble, Utility Dive, 23 March 2026). Setting it against the forecast window is KPA's comparison.

caption: curtailment that matches forecast data center growth, on paper
headline: Modest flexibility matches the data center forecast, on paper.
text: If data centers gave up 0.5% of their potential annual energy use, the existing grid could absorb about 98 GW, against roughly 90 GW of forecast data center growth for 2025–30. It does not cover total forecast growth of 166 GW, and in Texas forecast growth is about five times the 0.5% headroom.
source: KPA comparison of Duke University Nicholas Institute (February 2025) headroom with Grid Strategies (November 2025) forecasts. The Duke authors made a related point in 2025.

caption: of that headroom is under contract today
headline: Contracts cover about 1% of the headroom.
text: Google had contracted about 1 GW of data center demand response across five utilities by March 2026, roughly 1% of the most conservative headroom figure of 76 GW.
source: KPA calculation on Google (March 2026) and Duke University Nicholas Institute figures.

caption: rise in PJM's capacity price in two auctions, as reported
headline: A price signal that arrives all at once.
text: PJM's capacity price rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024/25 to $329.17 for 2026/27, an 11-fold increase, and it has cleared at the cap of a price collar in each of the last three auctions. Its market monitor attributes $29.4 billion, or 46%, of the cost of the last four auctions to data center load.
source: Reported figures, not a KPA finding: PJM auction results; IEEFA (July 2025) made the same comparison; Monitoring Analytics via Utility Dive, July 2026.

caption: likely data center requests against forecast growth
headline: The queue is not the load.
text: Wood Mackenzie counts 1,066 GW of US data center interconnection requests. Even the 28% it expects to be served, about 300 GW, is more than three times the roughly 90 GW of data center growth in utilities' own forecasts. Against the raw total the ratio is about 12 to 1, though the definitions do not match.
source: KPA comparison of Wood Mackenzie (via Capacity, 25 August 2026) with Grid Strategies (November 2025).

caption: of a utility's peak, drawn by one campus
headline: One customer, roughly half a utility.
text: Meta's Hyperion campus in Louisiana is described at 5 GW or more. Entergy Louisiana's peak in the record heat of August 2023 was about 10.3 GW.
source: KPA pairing of Louisiana Illuminator (5 August 2026) and Entergy 2023 peak data. Similar comparisons ran in Sierra (2025) and Fortune (2026).

caption: of the Texas large-load queue has passed stability study
headline: Texas has barely begun to clear its queue.
text: Of the 474 GW in the Texas large-load queue, only about 6.6 GW had passed the grid operator's new stability study by August 2026, and none of those had been approved to switch on. About 8.9 GW had been approved to energize under ERCOT's earlier process.
source: KPA division of figures reported by Utility Dive (21 August 2026); ERCOT, June 2026, for the earlier process.

caption: added to household price rises by being in PJM, 44 states
headline: The bill lands on the region, not the host state.
text: Several independent analyses this year found that data center concentration does not explain which states' household prices rose fastest, and that being in PJM does; OpenData Labs put it most plainly in July. KPA's regression on 44 states agrees and sizes the regional effect: being in PJM adds about 17 percentage points (p = 0.002), while data center share has no significant effect.
source: The pattern was published first by OpenData Labs (July 2026), IER, Heatmap, CRA and LBNL. The regression is KPA's, on EPRI and EIA data.
